Maximum likelihood population effects (MLPE) measurement model

Source: R/mlpe.R
mlpe.Rd

A function of class "terradish_measurement_model" that evaluates the maximum likelihood population effects (MLPE) likelihood. MLPE accounts for the non-independence of pairwise genetic distances that share a sampling site. It is the preferred distance-response likelihood when a defensible effective Wishart degrees-of-freedom value is unavailable or the response is not admissible for generalized_wishart.

Usage

mlpe(
  E,
  S,
  phi,
  nu = NULL,
  gradient = TRUE,
  hessian = TRUE,
  partial = TRUE,
  nonnegative = TRUE,
  validate = FALSE
)

Arguments

E

Conductance-implied covariance matrix: the generalized inverse of the graph Laplacian, evaluated at the current conductance parameters. Passed automatically by the optimizer; users normally do not call this function directly.

S

Square, symmetric matrix of observed pairwise genetic distances (e.g. \(F_{ST}\)). Must have the same dimensions as E.

phi

Named numeric vector of nuisance parameters (alpha, beta, tau, rho). The stored tau is log precision and the stored rho is an unconstrained, logit-scale parameter. Omit to obtain starting values from a least-squares fit and a weak positive MLPE correlation.

nu

Unused; present for a common interface with Wishart measurement models.

gradient

Logical. Compute gradient of the negative log-likelihood with respect to phi?

hessian

Logical. Compute Hessian of the negative log-likelihood with respect to phi?

partial

Logical. Compute second partial derivatives with respect to phi, E, and S? Required by the optimizer.

nonnegative

Logical. Constrain the IBR slope beta to be nonnegative? Default TRUE.

validate

Logical. Numerically validate gradients and Hessians via numDeriv? Very slow; for debugging small examples only.

Value

When phi is missing, a list with elements phi (starting values), lower, and upper (parameter bounds). Otherwise a list containing:

objective

Negative log-likelihood.

fitted

Matrix of expected genetic distances (same dimensions as S).

boundary

Logical; TRUE if beta = 0, indicating no detectable IBR signal.

gradient

Gradient with respect to phi (if gradient = TRUE).

hessian

Hessian matrix with respect to phi (if hessian = TRUE).

gradient_E

Gradient with respect to E (if partial = TRUE).

partial_E

Jacobian of gradient_E with respect to phi (if partial = TRUE).

partial_S

Jacobian of gradient with respect to the lower triangle of S (if partial = TRUE).

jacobian_E

Function for reverse-mode AD through E (if partial = TRUE).

jacobian_S

Function for reverse-mode AD through S (if partial = TRUE).

Details

The likelihood uses maximum likelihood (ML), not restricted maximum likelihood (REML). AIC can therefore compare different conductance formulas fitted to the same response, sites, graph, and likelihood family. That comparison does not validate the correlation model: in unpublished development simulations, model-based standard errors understated replicate variation about 1.7-fold. Use spatial CV to assess out-of-sample support for conductance terms.

With the standard nuisance bounds, fitting profiles the regression coefficients and residual precision analytically at each shared-site correlation, then searches the correlation before Newton refinement. The resistance predictor is centered and scaled internally so changing its units does not change the nuisance optimum or convergence criterion. Stored coefficients remain in the original units. Fixed predictive parameters and custom nuisance bounds use their supplied constraints. A profile reaching the upper numerical correlation endpoint is rejected because a regular finite nuisance optimum has not been established.

summary() reports rho on its internal logit scale, with a Wald interval on that scale. Convert an estimate or interval endpoint with plogis(rho) / 2 to obtain the shared-site correlation, which lies between 0 and 0.5. A value near 0.5 means site identity explains most of the residual variation. When the correlation approaches zero (fitted internal logit below -8), the logit parameter is poorly identified, so summary() reports rho as 0 with no standard error and prints a boundary note. The parameter remains in the degrees of freedom because it was estimated; fixing it in advance would define a different model. This boundary differs from a zero resistance coefficient, which leaves conductance unidentified.

To read the other nuisance parameters, alpha is the expected genetic distance at zero resistance distance, beta is the increase in genetic distance per unit of resistance distance, and the residual standard deviation is exp(-tau / 2).

The nuisance parameters are:

alpha

Intercept of the mean structure.

beta

Resistance-distance (IBR) slope; constrained \(\geq 0\) when nonnegative = TRUE.

tau

Log-precision parameter: residual variance is \(\exp(-\tau)\). In the Wishart measurement models the same name denotes a different quantity, the multiplier on graph covariance (see wishart_covariance).

rho

Unconstrained optimization-scale parameter. The actual shared-site correlation is \(\rho_{MLPE} = \text{plogis}(\rho)/2 \in (0, 0.5)\).

The mean structure is \(S_{ij} = \alpha + \beta R_{ij} + e_{ij}\), where \(R_{ij}\) is the resistance distance derived from E. The residual vector \(e\) follows the MLPE correlation structure of Clarke et al. (2002): two pairs \((i,j)\) and \((i,k)\) sharing site \(i\) have correlation \(\rho_{MLPE}\), while pairs sharing no site are uncorrelated.

Use mlpe_covariates to extend the mean structure with additional fixed pairwise covariates (isolation by environment). Coefficients describe conditional associations under the specified mean and correlation structure; they do not isolate causal environmental effects.

Worked example

vignette("v03-mlpe-pairwise-distance", package = "terradish") fits and interprets MLPE models for a pairwise \(F_{ST}\) matrix.

References

Clarke RT, Rothery P, Raybould AF (2002). Confidence limits for regression relationships between distance matrices: estimating gene flow with distance. Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics, 7, 361–372. doi:10.1198/108571102320 .

See also

leastsquares, mlpe_covariates, generalized_wishart, terradish

Examples

library(terra)

data(melip)
covariates <- c(terra::unwrap(melip.altitude),
                terra::unwrap(melip.forestcover))
coords <- terra::unwrap(melip.coords)
names(covariates) <- c("altitude", "forestcover")
# Coarsened so the example runs quickly; name layers, then scale.
covariates <- scale_covariates(terra::aggregate(covariates, fact = 3,
                                                na.rm = TRUE))
# Keep one site per raster cell (some melip sites share a cell).
keep <- !duplicated(terra::cellFromXY(covariates, terra::crds(coords)))
coords <- coords[keep]
Fst <- melip.Fst[keep, keep]
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords)

# Graph covariance (generalized inverse of the graph Laplacian) among the
# focal sites under uniform conductance (all coefficients zero).
laplacian_inv <- terradish_distance(theta = matrix(0, 1, 2),
                                    formula = ~ forestcover + altitude,
                                    data = surface,
                                    covariance = TRUE)$covariance[, , 1]

# Without 'phi': starting values and bounds for the nuisance parameters
mlpe(laplacian_inv, Fst)
#> $phi
#>       alpha        beta         tau         rho 
#>  0.01002299  0.22923592  6.47733469 -1.38629436 
#> 
#> $lower
#> [1] -Inf    0 -Inf -Inf
#> 
#> $upper
#> [1] Inf Inf Inf Inf
#> 
# With 'phi': the negative log-likelihood and derivatives at those values.
# qlogis(2 * 0.2) sets the actual shared-site correlation to 0.2.
value <- mlpe(laplacian_inv, Fst,
              phi = c(alpha = 0, beta = 0.5, tau = -0.1,
                      rho = qlogis(2 * 0.2)))
value$objective
#>       tau 
#> -58.01211
